followUps:
It resolves one path component at a time, starting from the root inode. Each directory is a file of (name, inode number) pairs, so the kernel reads the directory's data, finds the name, and loads that inode.

For /a/b/c: take the root inode (fixed number, e.g. 2), search it for a, load a's inode and check it is a directory with search permission, search it for b, then for c. That is 3 directory lookups, each needing the inode plus at least one data block (about 6 reads when cold). Mount points and symlinks add extra jumps.

The dentry cache is an in-memory cache of recent name-to-inode lookups, so the kernel does not re-read directories from disk on every path walk.

Each dentry links a parent, a name and an inode. It also stores negative entries for names known not to exist, which makes repeated failed open calls cheap. A warm lookup of /a/b/c becomes 3 hash-table hits instead of several disk reads. Dentries are reclaimed under memory pressure, and drop_caches can clear them.

code.title: Max file size with indirect pointers
code.python:
block, ptr = 4096, 4
k = block // ptr                  # pointers per block
direct = 12 * block
single = k * block                # each level multiplies reach by K
double = k ** 2 * block
triple = k ** 3 * block
print("K =", k)
print("direct =", direct)
print("single =", single)
print("double =", double)
print("triple =", triple)
print("total  =", direct + single + double + triple)

followUps:
The maximum file size drops sharply, because with 8-byte pointers a 4 KB block holds only 512 pointers, so K halves.

Now K = 512: single = 512 × 4 KB = 2 MB, double = 512² × 4 KB = 1 GB, triple = 512³ × 4 KB = 512 GB. The total is about 513 GB instead of 4 TB, roughly 8 times smaller, since the triple term scales with K³ (2³ = 8). Wider pointers address more blocks but shrink the fan-out.

Four reads in the worst case for the last byte in the triple-indirect range, plus the data block, so 5 in total when nothing is cached.

Cold path: read the inode (1), which holds the triple-indirect pointer; read the triple-indirect block (2); read the double-indirect block it points to (3); read the single-indirect block (4); finally read the data block (5). In the direct range it would be 2 reads (inode, data). In practice the inode and top-level index blocks are cached, so deep files cost far less.

code.title: Hard link vs symlink after deleting the original
code.python:
import os, tempfile

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
orig, hard, sym = (os.path.join(d, n) for n in ("orig", "hard", "sym"))
with open(orig, "w") as f:
    f.write("hello")
os.link(orig, hard)              # second directory entry, same inode
os.symlink(orig, sym)            # new file that stores the path "orig"
print("same inode:", os.stat(orig).st_ino == os.stat(hard).st_ino)
print("link count before:", os.stat(orig).st_nlink)
os.remove(orig)                  # removes one name only
print("link count after:", os.stat(hard).st_nlink)
print("hard link reads:", open(hard).read())
print("symlink dangling:", not os.path.exists(sym), "(islink=%s)" % os.path.islink(sym))
try:
    open(sym)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("opening symlink -> FileNotFoundError")

followUps:
Directory hard links could create cycles, and a cycle breaks both reference counting and tree walks.

If /a/b had a hard link /a/b/loop back to /a, then find, du and fsck would recurse forever, and after rm of the outside name the link counts would never reach 0, leaking the whole subtree. The kernel only allows the special entries . and .., which it manages itself. Symlinks are allowed because they are not counted references and tools can detect or skip them.

A process holding an open file descriptor keeps the inode alive even after the last name is removed.

The file is freed only when the link count is 0 and no open file descriptions remain. So rm on a log file that a daemon still writes to removes the name, but the data keeps growing and the disk space is not returned until the daemon closes or restarts. You can still read it through /proc/PID/fd/N. Programs use this trick for safe temporary files: open, then unlink immediately.

ext4 uses indexed allocation, in the form of extents, not one pointer per block.

The inode holds a small tree whose leaves are extents: (starting logical block, length, starting physical block). One extent can describe up to 128 MiB of contiguous 4 KB blocks, so a 1 GB contiguous file needs about 8 extents instead of 262,144 pointers. The allocator also tries to place data contiguously (multi-block allocation, delayed allocation), getting much of contiguous allocation's speed while keeping indexed flexibility.

A bitmap needs 1 bit per block, which is 32 MB for a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks.

Blocks: 1 TB / 4 KB = 240 / 212 = 228 = 268,435,456. At 1 bit each that is 228 / 8 = 225 bytes = 32 MB. Compare a free list with 4-byte pointers: 1 GB. Bitmaps also make it easy to find a run of free blocks, which helps contiguous allocation.

code.title: Write-ahead journal: crash at each stage

followUps:
Metadata journaling logs only structural changes (inodes, bitmaps, directories); data journaling logs file contents too.

Metadata-only is faster because file data is written once. It keeps the file system consistent (no lost inodes or double-allocated blocks) but a crashed append might leave the file with stale data in the new region. Data journaling writes every data block twice (journal, then home), roughly halving write throughput, but gives the file the state of the last committed transaction. Most systems default to metadata-only.

Because disks and SSDs reorder writes and cache them in volatile memory, the commit record could reach the platter before the logged blocks.

If the commit record lands first and power fails, recovery sees a commit, replays blocks that were never actually written, and corrupts the file system. So the sequence is: write log blocks, flush (barrier), write the commit record, flush. Each flush costs roughly one device round trip (tens of microseconds on NVMe, milliseconds on HDD). Checksums on the transaction can replace the first flush.

Copy-on-write (CoW) file systems never overwrite live blocks, so they need no separate journal.

A change writes new blocks, then new parents up to the root, and a single atomic update of the root pointer (uberblock/superblock) commits the whole tree. A crash leaves either the old root or the new one, both consistent. Cost: write amplification up the tree and fragmentation. Gains: free snapshots (keep the old root) and checksums on every block. ZFS and Btrfs work this way.

Delayed allocation postpones choosing disk blocks until writeback, which widens the window where data exists only in memory.

The file's size and extent are decided later, so a program that writes then crashes 20 seconds before the flush can lose the whole file even though write() returned. The famous case was ext4 truncating a file on rename without fsync, leaving zero-length files. ext4 now forces data out on a replace-via-rename pattern. The benefit is larger contiguous extents and less fragmentation.

A database knows its own commit order and needs durability exactly when it says, which the file system cannot guess.

The WAL gives the database atomic transactions and crash recovery independent of the file system mode: log record plus fsync means committed, and data pages can be written lazily and fixed up by replaying the log. It also turns random page updates into one sequential append. Relying on ext4 ordered mode alone would not protect multi-page updates (torn pages), so doing it in the database is required.

code.title: Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, LOOK
code.python:
head, edge = 53, 199
q = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67]
print("head=%d queue=%s" % (head, q))
# FCFS: serve in arrival order
fcfs, pos = 0, head
for r in q:
    fcfs += abs(r - pos); pos = r
# SSTF: always pick the nearest pending request
pending, sstf, pos = list(q), 0, head
while pending:
    r = min(pending, key=lambda x: abs(x - pos))
    sstf += abs(r - pos); pos = r; pending.remove(r)
# SCAN/LOOK going up first, then back down to the lowest request
hi, lo = max(q), min(q)
scan = (edge - head) + (edge - lo)   # SCAN runs to the disk edge
look = (hi - head) + (hi - lo)       # LOOK turns at the last request
print("FCFS=%d SSTF=%d SCAN=%d LOOK=%d" % (fcfs, sstf, scan, look))

followUps:
SSTF and, to a lesser degree, SCAN-style schedulers can starve requests; FCFS cannot.

SSTF always picks the nearest request, so with head at 53 a stream of new requests around 60 to 70 can keep a request at cylinder 183 waiting forever. SCAN and C-SCAN guarantee a bounded wait: the head must finish a sweep, at most about 2 × 199 = 398 cylinders of travel before any request is served. LOOK has the same guarantee. Only SSTF has unbounded wait.

C-SCAN gives the most uniform wait times.

SCAN favors the middle: a request just behind the head must wait for a full trip to the edge and back, while middle cylinders are visited twice per cycle. C-SCAN treats the disk as a circle and sweeps one direction only, so every cylinder is visited once per cycle, at equal intervals. With 200 cylinders each request waits at most about one sweep. The price is the long return jump, which does no useful work.

Mostly no: SSDs have no head, so there is no seek distance to minimise.

Access time is almost the same for any address, so ordering by cylinder gives nothing. What helps instead is merging adjacent requests, keeping the queue deep enough to use parallel flash channels, and avoiding starvation. That is why NVMe uses the none scheduler and SATA SSDs use simple deadline schedulers. SCAN-like logic still matters for HDDs and arrays of them.

Request merging combines adjacent requests into one larger I/O before sending it to the device.

Example: reads of sectors 100 to 107 and 108 to 115 become one read of 100 to 115. That gives one command, one interrupt and better sequential throughput instead of two. Linux does back merges (new request extends the end of a queued one) and front merges (extends the start) in the block layer. It helps HDDs a lot and SSDs somewhat, since per-command overhead matters at high IOPS.

mq-deadline gives every request an expiry time and serves expired requests first, even if sorting would delay them.

Requests sit in a sector-sorted queue for efficiency and in two FIFO queues (read, write) ordered by deadline. Default expiry is about 500 ms for reads and 5 s for writes, so reads are favored, since processes block on them. If the head of a FIFO has expired, the scheduler serves it next. It also limits how many reads can pass writes in a row, so neither side starves.

Because rebuilding a big disk takes a long time during which a second failure or read error destroys the array.

A 16 TB disk at 150 MB/s needs about 16,000,000 MB / 150 = 107,000 s, around 30 hours of rebuild, longer under load. With 1 URE per 1014 bits (about 12.5 TB), reading several 16 TB survivors will probably hit an unrecoverable error, and RAID 5 has no spare parity to fix it. RAID 6 or 10, or smaller disks, reduce the risk.

RAID 10 is a stripe of mirrors; RAID 0+1 is a mirror of stripes. They look similar, but RAID 10 tolerates failures better.

With 4 disks: RAID 10 = stripe over (A,B) and (C,D); after A fails, only B is critical, and a second failure kills the array only if it is B (1 of 3 disks). RAID 0+1 = mirror of stripe (A,C) and stripe (B,D); when A fails the whole stripe (A,C) is lost, so a second failure of B or D (2 of 3) kills it. Rebuild is also smaller in RAID 10: one disk copy.

code.title: RAID 5 parity rebuild and small write
code.python:
def bits(v):
    return format(v, "03b")

d0, d1, d2 = 0b101, 0b011, 0b110
p = d0 ^ d1 ^ d2                     # parity written for the stripe
print("D0=%s D1=%s D2=%s P=%s" % (bits(d0), bits(d1), bits(d2), bits(p)))
# disk 1 fails: XOR of every survivor, parity included, gives it back
rebuilt = d0 ^ d2 ^ p
print("D1 lost, rebuilt = %s ok=%s" % (bits(rebuilt), str(rebuilt == d1).lower()))
# small write: new parity from old data, new data and old parity only
new_d0 = 0b111
new_p = p ^ d0 ^ new_d0
print("small write P=%s full recompute=%s" % (bits(new_p), bits(new_d0 ^ d1 ^ d2)))

followUps:
Read only the old data block and the old parity block, then XOR: new parity = old parity ⊕ old data ⊕ new data.

Example with 3 bits: old D0 = 101, new D0 = 111, old P = 000. New P = 000 ⊕ 101 ⊕ 111 = 010. Cost: read 2, write 2, so 4 I/Os per small write, regardless of how many disks are in the array. The program above checks this equals a full recompute. This is the RAID 5 small-write penalty.

The write hole is a crash between writing the data block and the parity block, leaving the stripe's parity out of step with its data.

Everything looks fine until a disk fails; then the rebuild uses stale parity and silently produces wrong data for blocks that were never even being written. Fixes: a write-ahead log or journal for stripes, battery-backed cache, or full-stripe copy-on-write (ZFS RAID-Z). Linux md offers a write journal for this.

code.title: Atomic durable file replace with fsync
code.python:
import os, tempfile

def atomic_write(path, data):
    d = os.path.dirname(path)
    tmp = path + ".tmp"
    fd = os.open(tmp, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)
    try:
        os.write(fd, data)        # lands in the page cache only
        os.fsync(fd)              # force file data to stable storage
    finally:
        os.close(fd)
    os.rename(tmp, path)          # atomic on POSIX: readers see old or new
    dfd = os.open(d, os.O_RDONLY)
    try:
        os.fsync(dfd)             # make the rename itself durable
    finally:
        os.close(dfd)

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
target = os.path.join(d, "config.txt")
atomic_write(target, b"version=1\n")
atomic_write(target, b"version=2\n")
print("content:", open(target).read().strip())
print("leftover temp file:", os.path.exists(target + ".tmp"))

followUps:
fsync flushes data and all metadata needed to find it; fdatasync skips metadata not needed to read the data back; O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache.

Appending to a file changes its size, so fdatasync still flushes the size, but a pure overwrite of existing blocks avoids a journal commit for timestamps, so it can be about 2 times faster. O_DIRECT transfers straight between user buffer and device with aligned buffers and sizes (for example 4096), but it does not guarantee durability by itself; the device cache still needs a flush (or O_DSYNC).

Fsyncgate (2018) was the discovery that after a failed fsync, Linux could mark dirty pages clean, so a retry succeeded without the data being written.

PostgreSQL had retried fsync on error, assuming the data was still dirty, and could therefore lose committed data silently. The lesson: treat any fsync error as fatal, do not retry, and recover from the log. Kernel behaviour was improved, and PostgreSQL now panics on fsync failure.

Group commit lets many transactions share one fsync, so the expensive flush is paid once for the whole batch.

If one flush takes 1 ms, committing one transaction at a time gives at most 1,000 commits/s. When 50 transactions arrive during that millisecond and are flushed together, throughput becomes about 50,000 commits/s, with each transaction waiting at most about 1 to 2 ms. The log is sequential, so the batch is one large write.

Level-triggered epoll reports a descriptor as long as it is ready; edge-triggered reports only when it changes from not ready to ready.

If 100 bytes arrive and you read 40, level-triggered fires again on the next epoll_wait because 60 bytes remain. Edge-triggered stays silent, so you must read until EAGAIN, and the socket must be non-blocking. Edge mode means fewer wakeups but easier bugs (stalled connections from a partial read). Level mode is the safer default.

Node uses libuv: network I/O goes through epoll, but file I/O is done by a thread pool, since regular files cannot be polled meaningfully.

An fs.readFile call is queued to one of 4 worker threads (default UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE), which does a blocking read, then posts the result back to the event loop thread. So file I/O looks asynchronous to JavaScript but is blocking I/O hidden behind threads. Newer libuv can use io_uring on Linux for some operations.

An IOMMU translates and restricts the addresses a device uses for DMA, so a device can only touch memory it was given.

Without it a buggy or malicious device (or driver, or a compromised network card) can DMA over any physical memory, including kernel code. The IOMMU gives each device its own page table, like an MMU for peripherals. It also lets a VM own a physical device safely (passthrough) and lets devices use virtually contiguous buffers over scattered pages, at a small translation cost.

Both reduce the interrupt rate so the CPU is not overwhelmed at high packet or I/O rates.

At 10 Gbps with 64-byte packets there can be about 14.8 million packets per second; one interrupt each would use all the CPU. Interrupt coalescing makes the device wait (for example 50 microseconds or 32 packets) before raising one interrupt. NAPI switches the driver to polling once load is high: disable the interrupt, poll a budget of packets (for example 64) in a loop, then re-enable it when idle.

GPUDirect Storage lets the NVMe device DMA straight into GPU memory, skipping the bounce through CPU RAM.

The normal path is disk, to a page-cache or host buffer, then a CPU-driven copy across PCIe to the GPU, which uses host memory bandwidth twice. With a direct path the data crosses PCIe once, lowering latency and CPU load, which matters for loading large training datasets. It needs support from the driver, the file system and the hardware.

For a read-mostly archive I would choose capacity and cost over write speed: RAID 6 (or erasure coding) on large HDDs, with checksumming.

Writes are rare, so the RAID 6 write penalty (6 I/Os per small write) does not matter, while its capacity of (n−2)/n is good: 10 disks give 80% usable against 50% for RAID 10, and it survives two failures during the long rebuild. Use XFS or ZFS with checksums and scrubs to catch silent corruption, plus an off-site copy. fsync strategy is less critical, but verify files after writing.

Test them directly: pull the power during a write load and check that every acknowledged commit survives.

Tools such as diskchecker or pg_test_fsync run a writer against a second machine that records acknowledged sequence numbers; after a hard power cut the numbers on disk must match. Suspicious sign: fsync rates of 50,000 per second on a consumer SSD, which is faster than the flash can do, meaning the cache is lying. Prefer drives with power-loss protection capacitors, and check that the write cache setting is correct.
